learningObjective: Explain how a serving scheduler handles KV cache pressure via preemption / swap-out and its trade-offs.

canonicalClaims.claim: Under KV-cache pressure, the scheduler preempts selected in-flight sequences by either evicting (recompute on resume) or swapping their KV to host memory, admits new prefills into freed blocks, and resumes preempted sequences when capacity is available.
conditions: Paged KV cache with per-block allocation.
Scheduler has visibility into per-request KV footprint.
nonImplications: Does not imply preemption is free.
Does not imply every stack picks the same preemption policy.

misconceptions.claim: The scheduler overwrites old KV blocks in place to make room.
misconceptions.whyWrong: This would corrupt those sequences; correct behavior evicts or swaps, then resumes later.

misconceptions.claim: The scheduler compacts KV cache to defragment memory.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Paged KV eliminates external fragmentation, so compaction is unnecessary.

misconceptions.claim: The scheduler simply rejects new requests under pressure.
misconceptions.whyWrong: Serving stacks aim to keep utilization high; preemption and admission control are the standard levers.

implementationFacts: vLLM supports both recompute and swap policies configurable per deployment.
Swap requires PCIe copies to/from host memory; recompute pays the prefill cost again.
performanceScenarios: Long prompts favor swap (recompute is expensive); short prompts favor recompute (swap PCIe is comparatively costly).
